findings.finding: Neither an unnamed speaker nor pre-wedding composition logically contradicts Marie Antoinette origin. Narrative-before-birth timing is memoir framing and expressly may be anachronistic. Do not adopt contradicted origin from these premises.
findings.resolution: Use an evidence-limited origin judgment or narrow to what the checked narrative says; independent securely dated earlier attestations would address chronology, without automatically proving ultimate origin.

findings.finding: Selected passages do not identify Marie Antoinette as speaker. Utterance remains insufficient evidence within this package; author’s no-lifetime-source-found claim is a search report, not a universal negative.
findings.resolution: Say selected sources do not establish attribution; do not say never said it or imply exhaustive correspondence search.

findings.finding: Narrator’s first-part writing-place statement and later introduction are distinguishable. Introduction assigns Trye 1767–68 to second part, while institutional metadata dates the whole work 1765–1770. These do not pin the exact Book VI sentence to 1766–68.
findings.resolution: Keep composition range attributed and provisional; manuscript/critical-edition collation needed for precise passage date. Publication/transcription dates are not composition dates.

findings.finding: Birth/wedding dates support computed age 14 at wedding and ages 10–13 across 1766–68. Wedding is not arrival. No reintroduction of residence, food description, candidate-princess identity or unread earliest-attribution dates.
findings.resolution: Use supported dates and explicitly derived age; do not infer unprovided itinerary or biography.

findings.finding: The two language texts share a primary narrative, not independent witnessing. Official biography addresses chronology, not quotation attribution.
findings.resolution: Bind textual statements and date facts separately; do not let page counts create an independence tally.

limitations: A passage attributed to an unnamed princess does not identify her or prove the remark was actually uttered. It also does not prove that a different named person could never later repeat it.

Narrative time, recollection, composition, revision, publication and transcription/translation dates are separate. Pre-wedding writing plus childhood is not a logical disproof of coining a phrase; admitted anachronism also defeats treating the recalled pre-birth setting as independently established utterance timing.

The exact 1766–68 composition range for the quoted Book VI sentence is not securely established by the checked materials. Institutional whole-work metadata gives a broader range and manuscript variants; no original autograph or modern critical apparatus was read.

No comprehensive lifetime-attribution, correspondence, pamphlet or archive search was performed. Absence in selected sources is not proof of never uttering the words, and earliest source within this package is not universal first use.

French brioche and this English edition’s pastry are distinct wording from the popular cake question. No food-composition definition, identity of the princess, or universal translation equivalence is adopted.

Wikisource transcription and Gutenberg translation derive from the same Rousseau narrative. The later introduction is editorial chronology, not another witness. Versailles language versions share institutional source lineage.

Author-reported historical fetch prefixes/lengths and Britannica HTTP 403 remain attributed receipts; none was reproduced as a raw-byte acquisition in this review. Successful current text reads do not certify historical byte identity.
